title: Binary codes beyond the Gilbert–Varshamov bound
formal: Do constants \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\) and \(\eta >0\) and binary codes \(C_{n}\subseteq \{0,1\}^{n}\) for arbitrarily large n exist with minimum Hamming distance at least \(\delta n\) and \(\log _{2}|C_{n}|/n\ge 1- H_{2}(\delta )+\eta\)?
definitions: A code is any nonempty subset of the binary strings of length n; linearity, explicit construction and efficient decoding are not required. Hamming distance is the number of unequal coordinates, and minimum distance is the minimum over distinct codewords. \(H_{2}(t)=- t \log _{2}t- (1- t)\log _{2}(1- t)\). The constants \(\delta\) and \(\eta\) must be chosen before n and remain fixed along an unbounded sequence of block lengths. Finite-length improvements vanishing in normalized rate do not meet the target.

context_blocks.text: The Gilbert–Varshamov bound describes a rate-distance tradeoff achievable by random binary codes. Whether an asymptotically better tradeoff exists is a fundamental question about the information lost to adversarial errors.

This is a nonconstructive existence question, independent of whether codes meeting the bound can be efficiently written down. A polynomial improvement in the number of codewords at fixed length need not yield a positive constant improvement in rate. The coding-course materials distinguish these two open challenges.

why: Determine whether the basic random-coding benchmark is an intrinsic binary information limit.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.
